title: The root of all things
hook: the untaught make everything "mine", even nibbana; the monks were not pleased (MN 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle-Length Sayings. Your line: the middle length. Today, page one.

Most of the discourses end the same way: the monks were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One's words. It's the canon's standing ovation, again and again. The very first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends differently. The Buddha finishes speaking, and in the edition most translators follow, the text says plainly: the monks did not delight in what he said. First discourse. First page. Not pleased.
screen: `MOST DISCOURSES END DELIGHTED.` → `THE FIRST ONE DOESN'T.` → `NOT PLEASED.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Mulapariyaya, MN 1. The Buddha walks through everything a person could think of: earth, water, fire, air; beings and gods; the seen, the heard, the sensed, the known; unity and diversity; the all; and, last of all, nibbana. For each, he describes how an untaught person meets it. They perceive earth as earth. Then they conceive: they make earth into me, or put themselves in earth, or set themselves apart from it; they think, earth is mine, and delight in it. Why? Because they haven't fully understood it. The Pali verb is mannati: to conceive, to construe, to build a story with a self in it. And the startling part is the end of the list: even nibbana, the end of grasping, can be conceived and delighted in. Then someone in training, who knows earth directly as earth and is learning not to conceive. And the fully awakened, who don't conceive at all. Why weren't the monks pleased? The discourse doesn't say. A later commentary says these monks had been learned brahmins, proud of their scholarship, and the teaching was aimed at that pride. The Dhammapada makes a similar move, in Max Müller's translation: “These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,” with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth? Being bothered by a teaching sometimes means it found something.
screen: `EARTH, GODS, THE ALL, EVEN NIBBANA.` · `MANNATI — BUILDING A SELF-STORY.` · `KNOWING EARTH AS EARTH.` · `NOT PLEASED, ON PAGE ONE.` · then, large: `NOT PLEASED, YET.`

segments.voice: Let things come: a sound, a feeling in the body, a thought. Watch for the small move that follows, my knee, my plan, my noise, the word mine arriving half a second after the thing itself. You don't have to stop it; just see if you can catch the gap between the sound as sound, and then, mine.
Mannati, to conceive. How an untaught mind turns whatever it meets, even nibbana, into me and mine.
Your line: not pleased, yet. A teaching that bothers you can stay on the table a while. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monastics and scholars often study the Mulapariyaya Sutta as a famously difficult text; many teachers use it to point to the habit of making experience into 'me' and 'mine'.

fork.setup: the Buddha finishes the first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. how do the monks respond?
options: they delight in his words, as usual
they do not delight in his words
fork.reveal: they didn't delight. it's one of very few discourses that ends that way, and it sits on page one.

original.note: Pali maññati: to conceive, to construe; the verb MN 1 repeats for each thing the untaught make into 'me' and 'mine'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of philosophical categories.
what it means: how the mind turns whatever it meets into me and mine, even the highest goal.
what a scholar hears: the commentary says the listeners had been brahmins proud of their learning; its ending, 'the monks did not delight', is almost unique in the Pali discourses.

chat.says: What's the problem the Buddha points to in his very first discourse?
options: Seeing earth as earth, then building a me-and-mine story on top of it.
Seeing the earth at all; the senses themselves are the whole problem.
Not studying enough; the monks simply needed more learning first.
chat.meaning: In MN 1 the untaught person perceives earth as earth, then conceives it as me, in me, or mine, and delights in it.

Mulapariyaya.meaning: the root of all things, the first discourse of the Majjhima

mannati.meaning: to conceive: to build a story with a self in it

brahmins.meaning: members of ancient India's priestly class

sources.quoted: These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me, with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?
